The Long Road

By Sam Rivera

The road out of town begins as a wide avenue lined with plane trees, then narrows as the houses thin out and the fields begin. In spring the verges are thick with cow parsley, and the air smells of cut grass and wet earth. Cyclists pass in twos and threes, nodding to walkers who have the same idea about the morning.

After the second bridge the surface changes from tarmac to packed gravel, and the sound of the traffic falls away entirely. Here the river runs close beside the path, slow and brown, carrying leaves and the occasional feather. Herons stand in the shallows with the patience of statues, and lift off with a slow creak of wings when a dog comes too near.

The old mill marks the halfway point. Its wheel has not turned in sixty years, but the stones still hum faintly when the wind is right, or so the children say. A bench outside the mill is the customary place for the first sandwich, and the view from it takes in the whole valley, from the church spire in the east to the quarry scar in the west.

Beyond the mill the road climbs. It is not a hard climb, but it is a long one, and conversation dwindles to the essentials. The hedges give way to dry stone walls, the fields to rough pasture, and the sheep watch with the mild interest of creatures who have seen a great many walkers and been impressed by none of them.

At the top there is a cairn, and the tradition is to add a stone. Nobody knows when the tradition began or who began it, which is the way with the best traditions. From the cairn you can see the next valley, and the next road, and on a clear day the thin bright line of the sea.

The way back is quicker, as it always is. The light has moved round, the shadows of the walls lie the other way, and the town, when it comes into view again, looks smaller than it did in the morning, and more welcoming. The vote, when it came to naming the road, was unanimous: it would simply keep the name it had always had.
